questions.q: Find the intervals in which the function $f(x) = 5x^{3/2} - 3x^{5/2}$, $x > 0$, is (i) increasing (ii) decreasing.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — differentiate.**

$$f'(x) = 5 \cdot \frac{3}{2}x^{1/2} - 3 \cdot \frac{5}{2}x^{3/2} = \frac{15}{2}x^{1/2} - \frac{15}{2}x^{3/2}.$$

**Step 2 — factorise**, which is what makes the sign readable :

$$f'(x) = \frac{15}{2}x^{1/2}\left(1 - x\right) = \frac{15}{2}\sqrt{x}\,(1 - x).$$

**Step 3 — read off the sign.** For $x > 0$ the factor $\dfrac{15}{2}\sqrt{x}$ is always **positive**, so the sign of $f'(x)$ is decided entirely by $(1 - x)$ :

- $0 < x < 1$ : $(1 - x) > 0$, so $f'(x) > 0$ — **increasing**.
- $x = 1$ : $f'(x) = 0$ — a stationary point.
- $x > 1$ : $(1 - x) < 0$, so $f'(x) < 0$ — **decreasing**.

**Answer.**

(i) $f$ is increasing on $(0, 1)$.

(ii) $f$ is decreasing on $(1, \infty)$.

The function therefore has a maximum at $x = 1$, where $f(1) = 5 - 3 = 2$.

questions.q: The side of an equilateral triangle is increasing at the rate of 3 cm/s. At what rate is its area increasing when the side of the triangle is 15 cm? Give your answer in cm²/s, correct to two decimal places.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — write the relation.** For an equilateral triangle of side $a$,

$$A = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}a^2.$$

**Step 2 — differentiate with respect to time**, using the chain rule :

$$\frac{dA}{dt} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} \cdot 2a \cdot \frac{da}{dt} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\,a\,\frac{da}{dt}.$$

**Step 3 — substitute** $a = 15$ cm and $\dfrac{da}{dt} = 3$ cm/s :

$$\frac{dA}{dt} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times 15 \times 3 = \frac{45\sqrt{3}}{2} = 22 \cdot 5\sqrt{3}.$$

**Step 4 — evaluate.**

$$\frac{dA}{dt} \approx \mathbf{38 \cdot 97}\ \text{cm}^2\text{/s}.$$

Note that the answer depends on the side length at that instant — the area of a growing triangle speeds up as it gets bigger, because $A$ goes as $a^2$ while $a$ grows steadily.

questions.q: If $f(x) = a(x - \cos x)$ is strictly decreasing in $\mathbb{R}$, then $a$ belongs to :
questions.solution:
Differentiate :

$$f'(x) = a\left(1 + \sin x\right).$$

Now $\sin x \geq -1$ for every real $x$, so $1 + \sin x \geq 0$ always — it is zero only at isolated points where $\sin x = -1$.

For $f$ to be **strictly decreasing** we need $f'(x) \leq 0$ throughout (and not identically zero on any interval). Since $1 + \sin x$ is never negative, this forces

$$a < 0.$$

If $a > 0$ the function would be strictly increasing, and $a = 0$ makes $f$ constant — neither is decreasing. So $a \in (-\infty, 0)$.

questions.q: If the sides of a square are decreasing at the rate of $1 \cdot 5$ cm/s, find the rate of decrease of its perimeter, in cm/s.
questions.solution:
Let the side be $a$ and the perimeter $P$. For a square,

$$P = 4a.$$

Differentiate with respect to time :

$$\frac{dP}{dt} = 4\,\frac{da}{dt}.$$

The side is decreasing at $1 \cdot 5$ cm/s, so $\left|\dfrac{da}{dt}\right| = 1 \cdot 5$ and

$$\left|\frac{dP}{dt}\right| = 4 \times 1 \cdot 5 = \mathbf{6}\ \text{cm/s}.$$

The perimeter is decreasing at 6 cm/s. Note this does not depend on the size of the square — the relation $P = 4a$ is linear, so the rates are always in the ratio 4 : 1.

questions.q: If the distance travelled by a particle in $t$ seconds is given by $S = 72t + 3t^2 - t^3$, find the time, in seconds, taken by the particle to come to rest.
questions.solution:
The particle is at rest when its velocity is zero. Velocity is the derivative of distance :

$$v = \frac{dS}{dt} = 72 + 6t - 3t^2.$$

Set $v = 0$ :

$$72 + 6t - 3t^2 = 0.$$

Divide through by $-3$ :

$$t^2 - 2t - 24 = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (t - 6)(t + 4) = 0.$$

So $t = 6$ or $t = -4$. Time cannot be negative, so

$$t = \mathbf{6}\ \text{seconds}.$$

questions.q:
If $M$ and $m$ denote the local maximum and local minimum values of the function $f(x) = x + \dfrac{1}{x}$ $(x 
eq 0)$ respectively, find the value of $(M - m)$.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — stationary points.**

$$f'(x) = 1 - \frac{1}{x^2} = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x^2 = 1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x = \pm 1.$$

**Step 2 — classify them.** $f''(x) = \dfrac{2}{x^3}$.

At $x = 1$ : $f''(1) = 2 > 0$, so this is a local **minimum**, with $m = f(1) = 1 + 1 = 2$.

At $x = -1$ : $f''(-1) = -2 < 0$, so this is a local **maximum**, with $M = f(-1) = -1 - 1 = -2$.

**Step 3 — subtract.**

$$M - m = -2 - 2 = \mathbf{-4}.$$

This looks wrong at first glance — the local maximum value is **smaller** than the local minimum value. It is correct: the two stationary points sit on opposite branches of the curve, separated by the asymptote at $x = 0$, so neither is a maximum or minimum of the whole function.

questions.q:
Find the local minimum value of the function $f(x) = 4x^2 + \dfrac{1}{x}$ $(x 
eq 0)$.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — stationary points.**

$$f'(x) = 8x - \frac{1}{x^2} = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 8x = \frac{1}{x^2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 8x^3 = 1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x = \frac{1}{2}.$$

**Step 2 — classify.**

$$f''(x) = 8 + \frac{2}{x^3}, \qquad f''\!\left(\tfrac12\right) = 8 + 16 = 24 > 0,$$

so $x = \dfrac{1}{2}$ gives a local **minimum**.

**Step 3 — the value.**

$$f\!\left(\frac12\right) = 4 \times \frac14 + \frac{1}{1/2} = 1 + 2 = \mathbf{3}.$$

(There is no local maximum: $f'$ has only this one zero.)

questions.q: Find the absolute maximum and minimum values of the function $f(x) = 12x^{4/3} - 6x^{1/3}$, $x \in [0, 1]$.
questions.solution:
On a **closed** interval the absolute extremes occur either at a stationary point inside or at an endpoint, so find all three kinds of candidate.

**Step 1 — differentiate.**

$$f'(x) = 12 \cdot \frac{4}{3}x^{1/3} - 6 \cdot \frac{1}{3}x^{-2/3} = 16x^{1/3} - 2x^{-2/3}.$$

**Step 2 — stationary points.** Setting $f'(x) = 0$ and multiplying through by $x^{2/3}$ :

$$16x - 2 = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x = \frac{1}{8},$$

which lies inside $[0, 1]$.

**Step 3 — evaluate at every candidate.**

$$f(0) = 0,$$
$$f\!\left(\tfrac18\right) = 12\left(\tfrac18\right)^{4/3} - 6\left(\tfrac18\right)^{1/3} = 12 \cdot \frac{1}{16} - 6 \cdot \frac12 = \frac34 - 3 = -\frac94,$$
$$f(1) = 12 - 6 = 6.$$

**Step 4 — compare.**

The **absolute maximum** is $\mathbf{6}$, at $x = 1$.

The **absolute minimum** is $\mathbf{-\dfrac{9}{4}} = -2 \cdot 25$, at $x = \dfrac18$.

questions.q: Show that $f(x) = e^{x} - e^{-x} + x - \tan^{-1} x$ is strictly increasing in $\mathbb{R}$.
questions.solution:
A function is strictly increasing on $\mathbb{R}$ if $f'(x) > 0$ for every real $x$.

**Differentiate.**

$$f'(x) = e^{x} + e^{-x} + 1 - \frac{1}{1 + x^2}.$$

(The derivative of $-e^{-x}$ is $+e^{-x}$, and the derivative of $-\tan^{-1}x$ is $-\dfrac{1}{1+x^2}$.)

**Bound the two parts separately.**

First, by AM–GM applied to the positive numbers $e^x$ and $e^{-x}$,

$$e^{x} + e^{-x} \geq 2\sqrt{e^{x} \cdot e^{-x}} = 2.$$

Second, since $1 + x^2 \geq 1$ for every real $x$, we have $\dfrac{1}{1+x^2} \leq 1$ and therefore

$$1 - \frac{1}{1 + x^2} \geq 0.$$

**Add them.**

$$f'(x) \geq 2 + 0 = 2 > 0$$

for every $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

Since the derivative is strictly positive everywhere, $f$ is **strictly increasing on $\mathbb{R}$**.

questions.q: The maximum value of $\sin x + \cos x$ is:
questions.solution:
Write it as a single wave: $\sin x + \cos x = \sqrt{2}\,\sin\left(x + \tfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$.

A sine never exceeds $1$, so the maximum is $\mathbf{\sqrt{2}}$, reached at $x = \tfrac{\pi}{4}$.

Two waves of equal height a quarter-turn apart add up to one wave, taller by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$ — never to twice the height, because they never peak together.

questions.q: If $f'(c) = 0$ and $f''(c) > 0$, then at $x = c$ the function $f$ has:
questions.solution:
$f'(c) = 0$ says the tangent is flat; $f''(c) > 0$ says the curve is bending upwards there — a valley floor.

So $f$ has a **local minimum** at $c$. (Bending downwards, $f''(c) < 0$, would make it a peak.)

questions.q: Use differentials to find the approximate value of $\sqrt{36.6}$, correct to three decimal places.
questions.solution:
Take $y = \sqrt{x}$ with $x = 36$ and $\Delta x = 0.6$.

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} = \dfrac{1}{12}$.

$\Delta y \approx \dfrac{1}{12} \times 0.6 = 0.05$, so $\sqrt{36.6} \approx 6 + 0.05 = \mathbf{6.05}$.

(The true value is $6.0498\ldots$) The tangent line is a good stand-in for the curve as long as you do not walk far from the point of contact.

questions.q: A $5$ m ladder leans against a wall. Its foot slides away from the wall at $2$ cm/s. How fast (in cm/s) is the top sliding down when the foot is $3$ m from the wall?
questions.solution:
With $x$ along the ground and $y$ up the wall, $x^{2} + y^{2} = 25$.

Differentiate with respect to time: $2x\dfrac{dx}{dt} + 2y\dfrac{dy}{dt} = 0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{dy}{dt} = -\dfrac{x}{y}\dfrac{dx}{dt}$.

When $x = 3$, $y = 4$. So $\dfrac{dy}{dt} = -\dfrac{3}{4}(2) = -1.5$ cm/s.

The top slides **down** at $\mathbf{1.5}$ cm/s — the minus sign is the direction, the number is the speed.

questions.q: Find the absolute maximum and absolute minimum values of $f(x) = x^{3} - 3x$ on the interval $[-2, 3]$.
questions.solution:
On a closed interval the extremes can only sit at a critical point or at an endpoint, so check all of them.

$f'(x) = 3x^{2} - 3 = 0 \Rightarrow x = \pm 1$, and both lie inside $[-2, 3]$.

$f(-2) = -8 + 6 = -2$

$f(-1) = -1 + 3 = 2$

$f(1) = 1 - 3 = -2$

$f(3) = 27 - 9 = 18$

**Absolute maximum $= 18$ at $x = 3$; absolute minimum $= -2$, reached at both $x = -2$ and $x = 1$.**

The local peak at $x = -1$ is not the highest point on the interval — a local champion need not be the national one.

questions.q: The radius of a sphere is measured as $9$ cm with an error of $0.03$ cm. Find the approximate error in its calculated surface area.
questions.solution:
$S = 4\pi r^{2}$, so $\dfrac{dS}{dr} = 8\pi r$.

$\Delta S \approx 8\pi r\,\Delta r = 8\pi(9)(0.03) = \mathbf{2.16\pi}$ cm$^{2} \approx 6.79$ cm$^{2}$.

A small slip in the radius is magnified about $8\pi r$ times in the surface area — which is why measuring the radius carefully matters far more than it looks.
